The sunshine window

The fairies say sunlight is made of every colour at once, and they are right: a prism (or a rainbow) splits white light into red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. Isaac Newton showed this in 1666 with a glass prism in a dark room.

The queen's letters
A letter on the queen's desk
My dear Godmother, The ball was splendid. Everyone danced, nobody quarrelled, and the cake was taller than the King. Please come again at midnight; the pumpkins miss you. Your loving Queen
The Fairy Godmother's wands
🏰 Inside the dolls' castle there is a dolls' castle, and inside that... no, that's enough castles for one day.
The pixie-dust jars
🫧 Pop! Pop! Pop! Every bubble is round because a bubble's skin pulls itself as small as it can, and a sphere is the smallest skin that can hold the air inside.

🌸 Your petal spins down the fountain, round and round, three tiers to the bottom. In Faerie that means good weather for a week.

look out over Faerie

Far below: the toadstool village with its well, the fae market's stalls, the moonpool silver in the trees, the standing stones on the hill, and Titania and Oberon's glade where the fairy ring is. On a clear day you can see a unicorn. Today is a clear day.
The king's riddle book
🎶 The tiny dancer turns, and the music box plays a little waltz.

A kind girl kept in the cinders is helped by her fairy godmother: a pumpkin becomes a golden coach, mice become horses, and her rags become a gown. She dances with the prince, but must be home by midnight. She runs, and leaves a glass slipper on the stairs. The prince searches the kingdom until he finds the foot it fits.
Charles Perrault, 1697 (and the Grimms' Little Briar Rose)

At a princess's christening one fairy, left off the guest list, foretells she will prick her finger on a spindle. A kind fairy softens it: not death, but a sleep of a hundred years. It happens; the whole castle sleeps with her, and a wood of briars grows up round it, until a prince comes through.
The Brothers Grimm, 1812

A girl with wonderfully long golden hair is shut in a tower with no door and no stair. To visit, the witch calls: Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair! A prince overhears, climbs the braid himself, and in the end, after many troubles, the two find each other again.
Hans Christian Andersen, 1844

A splinter of a goblin's mirror gets into Kai's eye and heart, and the Snow Queen carries him off to her palace of ice. His friend Gerda walks the whole world to find him, helped by a reindeer and a robber girl, and her warm tears melt the splinter away.
The Princess and the Pea
Hans Christian Andersen, 1835

A soaked girl at the gate says she is a real princess. The queen puts one pea under twenty mattresses and twenty feather beds. In the morning the girl says she slept terribly: something hard was in the bed. Only a real princess could be so sensitive, so the prince marries her.

A miller's youngest son is left only a cat. The cat asks for boots and a bag, and by cleverness (and tricking a shape-changing ogre into turning into a mouse) wins his master a castle and the hand of a princess.
The Elves and the Shoemaker

A poor shoemaker cuts leather for one pair of shoes and goes to bed. In the morning the shoes are made, perfectly. Night after night it happens, until he and his wife stay up and see two little elves at work, and sew them tiny clothes to say thank you.
The Twelve Dancing Princesses
The Brothers Grimm, 1815

Every morning the twelve princesses' shoes are worn through, though their door was locked. A soldier with a cloak that makes him unseen follows them down a hidden stair, through woods of silver, gold and diamond trees, to a castle where they dance all night.
The Little Mermaid
Hans Christian Andersen, 1837

The youngest daughter of the sea king longs for the world above and saves a prince from a shipwreck. She trades her voice for legs. Andersen's ending is his own, gentle and strange: she becomes a daughter of the air.

A girl no bigger than a thumb is born from a flower. She is carried off by a toad, a beetle and a mole, saves a swallow through the winter, and the swallow carries her south to the land of flower fairies, where she gets wings.
Beauty and the Beast
Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumont, 1756
To save her father, Beauty goes to live in the castle of a beast who is kind and sad. She grows to love him for his goodness, and her love breaks the spell that made him a beast.

The royal floor: the Great Hall of Roses, the Glass Slipper Gallery, the Throne Room (kneel to be crowned), the Grand Ballroom (wind the music box and dance), the Banquet Hall and its great cake, the Wishing Well Court, the Room of the Magic Mirror, the Storybook Library, the Harp Room, the Treasury, the Butterfly Conservatory, the Toadstool Tea Room and the kitchens.

Up the stairs, the royal chambers: the Princess's and Prince's bedchambers, the Royal Wardrobe, the Fairy Godmother's Workroom with her pumpkin coach, the Gallery of Fairy Tales, the Pixie Loft, the Toy Room and the Nursery.

At the top, the tower tops: the Spinning Room (careful!), Rapunzel's Tower Room, the Star Tower, the Crown Jewel Room, the Sky Garden, the Bell Tower, the Potion Tower, the Dragon's Egg Room and the Snow Queen's Room. Look for the ✨ cards: everything glowing in a card can be done.
👠 The glass slipper fits! The herald gasps. The whole gallery bows to you. (It fits about one dreamer in three: a fairy slipper is generous.)

Your fairy fortune card
🎵 The golden harp sings. A harp's strings are different lengths: the shorter the string, the faster it shakes, and the higher the note.
I have keys but open no locks. I have space but no room. You can enter, but not go outside. What am I?
The more of me you take, the more you leave behind. What am I?
I am full of holes but I still hold water. What am I?
What has a neck but no head, and wears a cap?
What gets wetter the more it dries?
I go up and down the stairs without moving. What am I?
What can you catch but never throw?
I have a face and two hands, but no arms or legs. What am I?
What has one eye but cannot see?
What belongs to you, but other people use it more than you do?
“Right you are, and fairest in the land at riddles!”
“Not quite, dear dreamer. Think again.”
Try that one again
“Mirror, mirror, on the wall…” The glass ripples, and a voice answers with a riddle:
“Yes! You have it.”
📖 Right! The King would be delighted.
📖 Not that one. The answer was
a golden ball that once rolled into a well (the frog fetched it back)
a pea, very small and very important
a single bean that hums a tune
a tiny pair of elf's shoes
a feather from the swallow who carried Thumbelina
a key that opens nothing, and so opens everything
a ribbon from the twelve dancing princesses, worn through at the end
🗝️ You lift the lid. Inside, on red velvet:

A butterfly starts as an egg, hatches as a caterpillar, wraps itself in a chrysalis, and comes out with wings: four lives in one. The colours on its wings are made of thousands of tiny scales, like roof tiles; some colours are not paint at all, but light bouncing off the shapes of the scales.
🦋 You count eight butterflies circling the arches. One lands on your shoulder for a moment, then flies off again.
✨ The well keeps your wish safe. It has kept wishes for a thousand years, and it has never told one.
Crowned in the Throne Room

The Toadstool Tea Party
Which tea will you have?
🫖 Pink, sweet and warm. Rosehips are the fruit of the rose, and full of vitamin C.
🫖 It tastes of silver and smells of night. The pixies swear by it.
🫖 Cool and bright. Mint has been made into tea for thousands of years.

strawberry and cream
lemon and elderflower

a sky-blue sugar mouse

The batter's in, the oven's warm. Which icing?
🧁 Twelve fairy cakes, iced
The pastry cook's notes

Fairy bread for the ball: soft white bread, butter right to the edges, and a shower of hundreds-and-thousands. Cut into triangles. Serve before midnight. The great cake: five tiers, each a different flavour, iced the night before so the roses set.
💃 The great music box plays a waltz: one-two-three, one-two-three. Waltzes go in threes, and the waltz was the dance of the grand balls of the 1800s. Take a partner and turn about the floor!
Which gown for the ball?
Rose pink with silver stars
Sky blue with a sweeping train
Sunshine gold with puffed sleeves
Lilac with a cape of butterflies
Mint green with daisies
gown. You will be the talk of the ballroom.

A pumpkin in the corner turns golden, just for a moment.
Three mice in waistcoats peep out and bow.
A shower of silver sparkles drifts down, slowly, like snow.
Your shoes shine like glass. When you look again they are your own.
🌙 You sing a lullaby. The royal babies yawn, and so does the nursemaid.
pixie dust sparkles up and settles on your hair. You feel very slightly lighter.

An old woman in the tale said: never touch the spindle. Will you?
🧶 Very wise. The spinning wheel hums to itself, a little disappointed.
💤 Ouch, a tiny prick of the finger. Your eyes grow heavy. You sleep, and sleep...
🌹 ...a hundred years later (or so it feels) you wake in the Princess's Bedchamber. The whole castle yawns and stretches with you.
Pick a star, make a wish.
The North Star (Polaris) hardly moves all night, because it sits almost over the Earth's north pole. Travellers used it to find their way.
A star's twinkle is our air: its light wobbles as it comes down through the moving layers of the sky.
The Sun is a star. It just happens to be ours.
Some of the starlight you see left its star before your great-great-grandparents were born.
💛 “Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair!” The golden braid tumbles from its hook all the way to the floor. (In the Grimms' tale it was twenty ells long, about twenty metres.)

Its stones are real ones, the fairies say: ruby (red), sapphire (blue), emerald (green) and diamond . Ruby and sapphire are the same mineral, corundum, in different colours. Diamond is carbon, the same stuff as a pencil's lead, packed tight deep inside the Earth.
🔔 BONG... BONG... The great bell rings out over Faerie. Down in the village the gnomes look up and wave.

Here is the castle, and the lantern path down to Titania and Oberon's glade with its fairy ring. West: the toadstool village round its well. The fae market. The hollow tree and the moonpool, the standing stones on the hill, and the elven tree in the east. Somewhere off the edge of the map, the fairies say, is the Rainbow Toadstool that leads to the Kids Zone.
